title: Air-gapped deployment intake - MedTech Inc & Redwood
summary: Initial intake focused on MedTech's air-gapped on-prem constraints: no internet egress, signed offline update process, HSM/KMS integration, hardware constraints (power/cooling), and timeline for a pilot. AE introduced Redwood's product modes; SE drilled into packaging, driver updates, and benchmarking methodology. Action items and next steps agreed: security questionnaire, signed update flow doc, pilot scope and timeline, and an on-site/remote hardware validation window.
next_steps: Redwood to share air-gap deployment runbook and signed update options (Lena)
MedTech to provide hardware inventory and rack power/thermal constraints (Ben)
Redwood SE to schedule benchmark window with access method (Carlos)
Compliance to review SOC2/ISO artifacts and KMS/HSM integration guide (Maya)
Schedule follow-up pilot kickoff for week of 2025-03-24

Lena Park: Send air-gapped deployment runbook + template for signed update package by 2025-03-10

transcript:
[Meeting header]
Date: 2025-03-05
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 1:07:12
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Dr. Aisha Khan (CTO, MedTech), Ben Ortiz (Infrastructure Lead), Maya Singh (Compliance), Ravi Patel (Site Ops)

[00:00] Lena: Hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intro from our side — I'm Lena, I'm the account lead, and Carlos is our solutions engineer. We'll try to map your constraints to Private/on-prem options and see what a pilot could look like.
[00:11] Dr. Aisha: Thanks, Lena. Short intros from our side — I'm Aisha, CTO, overseeing ML apps in clinical imaging; Ben's our infra lead, Maya handles compliance, Ravi is site ops. We're evaluating options for air-gapped inference for a dev-to-prod pipeline for a regulated med device.
[00:28] Carlos: Great. Before we dive, can I confirm your hard constraints? I heard no internet egress from the inference cluster and all updates must be via signed artifacts — is that correct?
[00:35] Ben: Yes, exactly. Nothing leaves the isolated VLAN. We can't use cloud registries or pull updates directly. Everything needs to be staged through our secure lab and then physically transferred or pulled from an offline mirror.
[00:52] Maya: And from compliance — we need audit trails for any model changes, KMS-integrated key management, and attestations for crypto libraries (FIPS) and vendor proofs. SOC2 is baseline; ISO 27001 preferred.
[01:10] Lena: Understood. We deal with a lot of regulated shops — Redwood Private supports VPC/on-prem installs and we have an air-gapped packaging flow. To be clear, the packaging options are typically: signed OCI tarball we load into an offline registry, or a signed model bundle plus runtime assets that you push to a node. Both are viable.
[01:33] Ravi: How does the runtime handle GPUs and drivers when there's no internet? We have a mix of A100s and some H100s planned, but driver updates are tightly controlled by our platform team.
[01:45] Carlos: Good question. The main pieces are: NVIDIA driver + CUDA, optional RAPIDS/cuDNN stacks, container runtime (we support containerd and dockerd variants), and our runtime (the inference engine). For air-gapped installs, we provide a host-agent package and a driver bundle checklist. We don't install kernel drivers for you — you apply signed driver packages that we've validated compatibility against, then our agent verifies the driver versions at runtime. There's a small shim that checks driver ABI compatibility.
[02:10] Ben: So Redwood doesn't push drivers through the internet, we stage them locally and then run the compatibility check?
[02:15] Carlos: Exactly. You stage the driver and firmware image in your secure lab, run the validation tool, then the nodes are marked ready.
[02:21] Dr. Aisha: What about model updates? Clinical models will be updated quarterly, maybe monthly for some pipelines. We need to be able to audit who approved the model and have signed artifacts we can roll back to.
[02:32] Lena: Our rollout supports pinned model versions per route. For air-gapped, we sign model bundles with a customer-managed key or Redwood-signed key per agreement. We also expose a timeline and change log. The key integration with your HSM/KMS can be done via an on-prem HSM gateway or a hardware module if you have one.
[02:54] Maya: Do you support customer-managed keys (BYOK) that never leave the HSM? That's non-negotiable for our legal team.
[02:58] Carlos: Yes. We have two patterns: 1) Redwood stores only encrypted blobs and the decryption happens via your on-site KMS/HSM using proposals for attestation; 2) You run a small KMS proxy in the air-gapped network — it performs unwrap operations without outbound egress. In both flows, keys don't leave the HSM.
[03:15] Ravi: How do you handle model caching/KV warming in an air-gapped cluster? We can't rely on remote caching or CDN.
[03:22] Carlos: Our runtime has local KV cache and prefix cache warm-up tools. For the pilot we usually ship a cache snapshot as part of the model bundle so cold starts are predictable. You can also pre-warm caches via a synthetic workload we provide.
[03:36] Ben: Storage — do you require NFS? We tend to avoid network file systems in the regulated zone.
[03:41] Carlos: We can use local NVMe per node or an approved SAN. NFS is supported but not required. For air-gapped high-throughput, local NVMe with an orchestration layer is recommended.
[03:50] Dr. Aisha: On orchestration — does Redwood rely on Kubernetes? Our facility prefers minimal orchestration footprint; heavy k8s is a risk from ops perspective.
[03:58] Carlos: We support a few deployment topologies: Kubernetes Operator, a lightweight node agent orchestrated via systemd for bare-metal clusters, and a more managed appliance-style bundle. For regulated on-prem, many customers choose the node-agent + orchestration policy model to reduce k8s surface area.
[04:18] Lena: Quick clarifying Q: do you have an on-prem registry or mirror?
[04:22] Ben: Not currently. We use a sealed, air-gapped registry in another site sometimes but it's not standardized. Part of this project is to decide whether we standardize an offline registry or accept tarball pushes.
[04:33] Maya: From compliance — we need an end-to-end signed chain: who built, who validated, and who deployed. Do you have provenance tooling?
[04:40] Carlos: Yes, artifacts carry a signed provenance file with build metadata, checksums, and signer PKI. We can also integrate with your internal CI system to generate SBOM-like manifests.
[04:49] Dr. Aisha: Great. What about hardware constraints beyond GPUs? Our racks are in a constrained power envelope; we can't spin up 6x H100s per node. Thermal and power are main blockers.
[05:00] Ravi: And we sometimes get vendor GPUs with specific firmware versions that need special handling.
[05:06] Carlos: We recommend profiling on representative hardware. For throughput workloads, we often recommend A100 40GB or H100 with quantization. If you have power constraints, we can discuss mixed node pools: some nodes with compact footprints for latency-critical paths and separate nodes for batch workloads.
[05:22] Ben: Is mixed-architecture routing a first-class feature? Like route requests to lowest-latency node that fits SLA and cost?
[05:28] Lena: Yes, smart routing is in the platform — policies by latency, cost, and model variant. In air-gapped it works same, but routing is within your private network.
[05:35] Maya: Encryption at rest — are we able to use FIPS-certified crypto stacks?
[05:40] Carlos: We can run with FIPS builds for the crypto libraries and support FIPS-compliant KMS flows. We'll need to validate specific Linux distro and kernel options to ensure the FIPS mode works.
[05:52] Dr. Aisha: What about evidence for auditors? We need logs around model inference for debugging as well as privacy. Can you produce tamper-evident logs?
[06:00] Carlos: We produce structured telemetry and audit logs. For air-gapped deployments, logs can be pushed to your SIEM via an approved forwarder. Tamper-evidence can be achieved via signed audit bundles and retention policies. We can also integrate with your HSM-based signing service to sign log batches.
[06:16] Lena: I want to touch on update cadence. You said quarterly updates — what is your minimum acceptable maintenance window?
[06:23] Ravi: Usually 2 hours per node during off-hours, but we can cluster updates to multiple nodes to reduce total window. However, firmware updates sometimes require longer windows.
[06:33] Carlos: Our agent supports rolling updates and can do canary rollouts inside the air-gapped network. For firmware, you control that; we orchestrate the application-level rollout once the node is ready.
[06:42] Ben: Benchmarking — we need a clear methodology. We have latency p99 SLAs for some endpoints — sub-100ms for smaller prompts. Do you have numbers for A100/H100 single-request latency?
[06:52] Carlos: We have verified profiles — approximate single-token latencies depend heavily on sequence length and quantization. Rough ballpark: on well-tuned A100, a 2k-context LLM in int8 can hit low hundreds of milliseconds per request for the first token and lower for subsequent tokens with KV cache. We'll provide specific bench scripts for your model and synthetic prompts.
[07:08] Dr. Aisha: I want to call out data residency/regulatory risk: some outputs may be stored in logs. Can we selectively redact or avoid logging inference payloads?
[07:18] Carlos: Yes — configurable logging levels. Inference payloads can be disabled or tokenized before logging. We also support on-the-wire masking in the agent.
[07:28] Lena: Quick reality check — timeline. What's your target for pilot and what success metrics?
[07:33] Dr. Aisha: Pilot by end of March ideally, but we can push to April. Success: ability to run a defined model on-prem with p99 < 200ms for clinical routing, KMS integration with no key export, and signed update proof.
[07:44] Ben: Also prove we can run within our rack power budget for at least two representative nodes.
[07:50] Maya: And compliance will sign off on the audit trail and KMS flow.
[07:55] Carlos: All feasible. For pilot we'll want a two-node test cluster to validate installs, a lab-based update run, and a 48-hour stress run with telemetry.
[08:04] Lena: Ok, can I propose immediate next steps: 1) Redwood sends an air-gapped runbook and update packaging options; 2) MedTech sends hardware inventory and power/thermal constraints; 3) Redwood sends a benchmark plan and sample dataset for synthetic testing; 4) Compliance exchange of required attestations and legal contact for the BYOK flow.
[08:20] Dr. Aisha: That works. One question — do you support hardware attestation for nodes (TPM)? We require hardware identity for certain enclaves.
[08:28] Carlos: Yes, we can verify TPM quotes during node provisioning; the node agent can record attestation into the provenance file. We'll need your provisioning CA cert to validate quotes.
[08:36] Ravi: What about offline telemetry export — is there a recommended pattern for pulling logs out for long-term retention?
[08:42] Carlos: You can do signed bundle exports on schedule, or run a push to a staging appliance that is then physically transferred for long-term retention. It's what a lot of air-gapped shops do.
[08:54] Maya: Legal is going to ask about indemnities and liability for inference errors in clinical workflows. Is Redwood comfortable being in the loop?
[09:02] Lena: We're not a medical device vendor; we provide inference infra. Responsibility for clinical decisions stays with you. We'll provide SLAs around uptime and documented behaviors, but we'd need the legal team to align on liability. We can surface standard enterprise terms and add specific carve-outs.
[09:16] Dr. Aisha: Noted.
[09:20] Ben: One more technical — can Redwood run without root on the inference nodes? We have strict host hardening and minimize root-level daemons.
[09:29] Carlos: The agent needs elevated privileges for certain operations (device nodes, driver checks). That said, we can limit the surface area and provide an audited syscall list. We also support deployment inside an isolated container with controlled capabilities if that helps.
[09:45] Lena: We're approaching the top of the hour; let's quickly recap and assign owners.
[09:51] Lena: (recap) Redwood to send runbook, update packaging, benchmark plan, and list of required driver versions. MedTech to share HW inventory, compliance checklist, and schedule a pilot kickoff.
[09:59] Dr. Aisha: We'll try to get the inventory and compliance list by next week.
[10:04] Maya: I'll aggregate the compliance items and share a prioritized list.
[10:09] Ben: I'll pull rack PDU data and GPU model/firmware versions.
[10:15] Carlos: I'll prepare a draft benchmark plan and a synthetic prompt set; we can iterate.
[10:20] Lena: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up via email with the attachments. If it's okay I'll set the pilot kickoff tentatively for March 24th and send calendar invites.
[10:29] Dr. Aisha: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[10:31] Lena: End meeting.
